title: Core-memory coincident-current selection with dual-gate 3D cells, no tier decoders
idea: Revive core memory's X/Y coincident-current selection: each 3D cell's access device is a dual-gate thin-film transistor that conducts only when both its tier strap and its vertical pillar gate are at half-select level, so N tier straps plus M pillars address N x M cells with only N+M drivers. Half-selected cells see one gate on and stay off, exactly as half-selected cores stayed below coercive force.
why: Facts 2 and 7: removes per-tier word drivers and most staircase decode, cutting periphery from ~49% toward ~30% and lowering the tier count needed to break even below 26.

title: Bonded bit-planes sharing one base-die row decoder, core-stack style
idea: Treat each hybrid-bonded DRAM array die like a core-memory bit plane: dies are thinned to ~5 um and carry sub-micron through-die vias at mat edges so one row decoder/driver on the base logic die drives the same wordline in all 16 planes, while each plane delivers one bit slice of the word. Array dies keep only cells and sense amps.
why: Facts 6 and 7: deletes row decoders and charge pumps from 15 of 16 dies (~15-20% of each die), giving ~15-25% lower cost per bit for stacked DRAM.

title: Diagonal sense-wire bitline twisting across tiers for 4F2 open arrays
idea: Copy core memory's diagonal sense wire, which crossed cores in alternating polarity so half-select pickup cancelled: in a vertical-channel 4F2 array, each bitline pair swaps tier position and coupling polarity every 8 cells, so wordline kick and neighbor coupling arrive as common-mode at the sense amp. This gives folded-bitline noise immunity at open-bitline area.
why: Facts 1 and 4: ~30-40% less coupling noise lets Cs drop from ~5 fF toward ~3.5 fF (lower capacitor aspect ratio) while keeping 4F2 (33% less area than 6F2).

title: Field-emitter-array Williams tube writing charge spots on blanket film
idea: Revive the Williams tube and GE's BEAMOS: a CMOS die carrying a Spindt-tip field-emitter array (one tip per 64x64 spot patch, electrostatically deflected) is vacuum-bonded a few microns above an unpatterned MOS/dielectric target, writing bits as ~30 nm charge spots and reading them by beam-induced current. The storage plane has no lithographic cell, capacitor or access transistor.
why: Facts 1, 2 and 4: the storage layer needs zero masks and zero EUV; if 30 nm spots hold charge, density rivals DRAM at a fraction of capital per bit with ~50 ns beam-settle access.

title: Nano vacuum-channel triodes as zero-leakage access switches in BEOL tiers
idea: Bring back the vacuum tube at 20 nm: each 3D cell's access device is a vertical field-emission triode etched into dielectric (metal tip, gate ring, storage-node anode), needing no crystalline channel and leaking essentially nothing when off. Cells stack in 50+ BEOL tiers because no epitaxy or high-temperature anneal is required.
why: Facts 2 and 3: removes the single-crystal lateral transistor blocker for 3D and the <=13 fA leakage tail, stretching retention from 64 ms to minutes and cutting refresh energy (16-33% of idle) by >90%.

title: Vertical CCD strings: 3D NAND geometry clocked as charge-coupled DRAM
idea: Revive 1970s CCD serial memory inside a 3D-NAND-like stack: a vertical gate-all-around oxide-semiconductor or poly channel with 128 wordline tiers is clocked in three phases to shift charge packets up and down, with one sense/regenerate amplifier at the string foot. There is no per-cell contact, capacitor or access transistor, and bidirectional shifting halves average latency.
why: Facts 1, 2 and 7: cell area approaches 3D NAND bit density (~10x DRAM per mm2) and one sense amp serves 128 bits; ~60-130 ns access fits the DRAM-class window for streaming data.

title: Drum-era SOAP placement makes shift-register memories act random-access
idea: Revive the IBM 650's Symbolic Optimal Assembly Program, which placed each next instruction where the rotating drum would be when needed: a compiler/controller lays out tensors, KV-cache pages and weights in shift-register arrays (CCD strings, racetracks, delay loops) so the next word reaches the read port just in time, with out-of-order prefetch hiding the rest.
why: Lets transistor-free serial 3D arrays serve the predictable ~60-80% of AI memory traffic at effective 10-30 ns latency, unlocking 5-10x denser arrays for DRAM's job.

title: Bubble-memory major/minor loop organization for stacked skyrmion tiers
idea: Reuse the bubble chip's architecture: in each tier of a sputtered magnetic multilayer stack, skyrmions circulate in hundreds of parallel minor loops driven by spin-orbit current, and a block-transfer gate swaps a whole page into one major loop read by a single MTJ. One etch defines the loops through all tiers, so tiers are added by deposition, not masks.
why: Facts 4 and 7: one reader per ~1e5 bits collapses periphery and extra tiers cost deposition only; a dense second-tier working memory at ~100 ns page access.

title: Plated-pillar memory: circumferential magnetization lining 3D NAND-style holes
idea: Revive Univac/Bell plated-wire memory vertically: etch high-AR holes through a stack of word-strap tiers, ALD a soft magnetic shell, spacer and reference layer down each hole, and store bits as circumferentially magnetized ring segments under each strap, sensed non-destructively by the magnetoresistance of an axial read current. Closed-flux rings have no stray field, so hole pitch can be tight.
why: Facts 2 and 8: a deposition-built 3D cell with non-destructive read, no capacitor and near-unlimited endurance; 3D NAND-like density at ~20-50 ns reads.

title: Twistor helical-anisotropy nanowires that write and sense through every tier
idea: Revive Bell's twistor (magnetic tape wound helically on a wire): grow vertical nanowires whose magnetic shell has a helical easy axis set by a twisted strain field, so an axial bitline current plus one tier strap's field switches only the crossing, and readout uses the inverse-Wiedemann voltage pulse induced along the same wire.
why: Facts 2 and 7: transistor-free vertical array where each pillar is both write and sense line for all tiers; per-cell device count and periphery drop sharply if the twist works below 50 nm.

title: Core-rope via-programmed 3D weight store, one sense per rope
idea: Revive Apollo's core rope, where a bit was set by whether a wire threaded a core: inference weights are encoded by whether a BEOL via links a rope wire to a shared sense node, written by maskless laser/e-beam via patterning in a mature U.S. fab and stacked 16 metal decks high, with one sense amp per 64 rope wires. Static weights leave DRAM, which keeps only activations and KV cache.
why: Doing DRAM's job with less: weights are often >50% of inference DRAM; rope bits cost ~5-10x less than DRAM bits and need no EUV, capacitor or refresh.

title: Selectron-style binary-coded tier selection replaces staircase contacts
idea: Revive RCA's Selectron, whose grid bars picked one eyelet by binary coincidence: at each mat edge every tier's wordline passes through log2(N) series select transistors whose thresholds are binary-coded per tier with log2(N) chop masks (the mask-halving trick already used for staircases), so 7 complementary vertical select-gate pairs choose one of 128 tiers. Fourteen contacts replace 128 staircase landings.
why: Facts 2, 4 and 7: staircase area and contact count scale as log2(N) instead of N, making 100+ tier 3D DRAM affordable in area and mask count.

title: Extended-Core-Storage block tier: DRAM mats without column decoders
idea: Revive CDC 6600 Extended Core Storage, a huge bank used only for wide block moves: build a zero-EUV, >=18 nm DRAM die whose mats have no column decoders or column-select lines; every activation streams its full 8 KB row through a wide serializer to a CXL port for KV-cache, embedding and paging traffic.
why: Facts 4, 7 and 8: deletes column periphery (~10-15% of die), turns 128x overfetch into payload, and avoids EUV (~30% wafer-cost cut) for a cheap capacity tier.

title: Antiferroelectric imprint crosspoint revives Bell's 1952 BaTiO3 matrix memory
idea: Bell Labs' 1952 passive BaTiO3 crosspoint memory died from half-select disturb; revive it with imprint-shifted, ZrO2-rich antiferroelectric HZO whose double hysteresis loop gives a sharp switching threshold that V/3 half-select cannot reach, stacking 8 selectorless decks of 20 nm lines at <=400 C.
why: Facts 1, 2 and 4: effective ~0.5F2 per bit with no transistor or capacitor tower; AFE cycling (>1e12) plus wear leveling approaches DRAM endurance needs.

title: Transfluxor-inspired split-electrode ferroelectric cell with non-destructive read
idea: Revive the transfluxor, where the flux state around a major aperture blocked or freed switching around a minor one: a vertical ferroelectric capacitor has a large write electrode and a small adjacent read electrode, and the stored major domain's depolarizing field biases the minor region. Reading toggles only the minor region, which springs back, sensing state without disturbing the stored domain.
why: Fact 8: non-destructive read removes write-back energy and read fatigue; ~3-5x lower read energy, and ferroelectric endurance is spent only on real writes.

title: Parametron phase bits held by pumped NEMS beams in stacked cavities
idea: Revive Goto's parametron: each cell is a nanomechanical beam parametrically pumped at 2f by a tier-wide electrostatic line, ringing at f with phase 0 or pi and holding that bit as long as the pump runs. Tiers of vacuum-sealed beams stack in BEOL, and reads use phase-sensitive capacitive pickup on the bitline.
why: Facts 1 and 3: no capacitor charge wall and no refresh; hold power is set by beam Q (~1e4) through one shared pump rather than 46 fJ/bit refresh.

title: Esaki tunnel-diode bistable cells as stackable two-terminal static RAM
idea: Revive 1960s tunnel-diode memories: a BEOL-grown interband tunnel diode (oxide or 2D heterojunction) in series with a thin-film load has two stable operating points held by a shared standby-bias line, and 4-8 such decks stack as crosspoint static memory read by small current pulses.
why: Facts 1 and 3: no capacitor and no refresh; two-terminal decks dodge the 3D transistor blocker, viable if peak-to-valley ratio >10 keeps standby below DRAM refresh power.

title: Ferreed-like latching NEMS relays as access devices in 3D tiers
idea: Revive the Bell ferreed crosspoint (a reed latched by remanent magnetism) as each 3D cell's access device: a ruthenium-contact nanoelectromechanical relay with essentially zero off-current, built in BEOL tiers without single-crystal silicon or tungsten. With leakage gone, storage capacitors shrink to ~1-2 fF, sized only for read margin on short local bitlines.
why: Facts 1, 2 and 3: lifts the capacitor charge wall (AR from ~70:1 toward ~20:1), nearly eliminates refresh, and avoids China-dominated tungsten.

title: Ferrite flux-rod through the stack broadcasts data to all dies
idea: Revive the magnetic core threaded by many wires: one high-permeability ferrite-filled vertical via runs through a 16-die stack and each die's on-chip coil wraps it, so a transmit coil on the base die couples to every die at once like a shared core. Data moves inductively (broadcast writes, time-sliced reads), replacing most HBM data TSVs.
why: Fact 6: one flux rod replaces dozens of TSVs, cutting TSV keep-out area and the 20-30% TSV-related yield loss; HBM area per bit falls ~1.5x.

title: Atanasoff capacitor-drum brushes: sense amps commutated across mats
idea: Revive the Atanasoff-Berry Computer's capacitor drum, where a few brushes served thousands of capacitors: mats carry no local sense amps, and a small pool of sense amps is commutated across 8 mats through a low-capacitance charge-transfer bitline multiplexer that pre-amplifies before switching.
why: Fact 7: sense-amp count and pitch-matched area shrink ~8x, cutting periphery from ~49% toward ~30% at a modest bank-parallelism cost.

title: Vertical Bloch-line memory revived in stacked synthetic antiferromagnet films
idea: Revive Konishi's 1983 vertical Bloch-line memory: store bits as pairs of Bloch lines inside the domain walls of stripe domains in stacked perpendicular synthetic-antiferromagnet films, stepping them along the walls with in-plane pulse fields. The domain wall itself is the track, so no lithographic cell exists.
why: Density and capital intensity: bits at wall-internal scale (~10-20 nm) with tiers added by sputtering; a mask-light bulk working memory candidate.

title: Flood-gun self-restoring cells: global diode pump refreshes every bit
idea: Revive the Tektronix bistable storage tube, whose flood gun held every spot at one of two stable potentials without reading it: each cell gets a tiny vertical diode plus coupling-capacitor pump driven by a global AC 'flood' line, so leaked '1' cells are recharged and '0' cells clamped low, all in parallel without activating rows or sense amps.
why: Fact 3: replaces row-by-row refresh (46 fJ/bit, 10-20% bandwidth loss) with an array-wide, sense-free restore; refresh energy down ~5-10x.

title: Thermally drawn multimaterial fibers woven like core planes into memory
idea: Revive hand-woven core planes with fiber drawing: a macroscopic preform holding metal, dielectric and semiconductor features is drawn ~1000x down into kilometers of fiber with ~50-100 nm internal cell structures, then fibers are woven or bundled and sliced into dense 3D arrays. Patterning happens once in the preform, not per wafer.
why: Capital intensity and U.S. manufacturability: no EUV or per-wafer masks, built in fiber plants; cost per bit could drop >3x if drawn features stay uniform.

title: Bubble-memory boot-loop map lets 3D tiers ship with dead strings
idea: Bubble chips shipped with several percent of minor loops defective plus a boot loop telling the controller which to skip; do the same in 3D DRAM: each mat stores a triple-replicated map of bitline segments whose cells fail, and column logic skips them at full speed. Up to 1% failing cells per mat are masked at test and remapped in the field.
why: Facts 2 and 4: tolerating 1% bad cells lets low-quality poly/oxide channels and 100+ tiers yield, cutting capital per good bit and the 3D break-even tier count.

title: Delay-line recirculation with decode-and-correct at every string lap
idea: Mercury delay lines regenerated every pulse on each lap; revive that in shift-register 3D strings: as data pass the string-foot regenerator, a short BCH codeword is decoded and rewritten corrected every lap (~1 us), so per-transfer and leakage errors of up to 1% per cell never accumulate.
why: Facts 2 and 3: allows leaky, trap-rich channels and 128+ tier strings, while refresh becomes free scrubbing; near-NAND density for working memory.

title: Core-style low selection ratio crosspoint that accepts and scrubs disturbs
idea: Core memory lived with a 2:1 selection ratio; build a 16-deck passive crosspoint of plain ferroelectric capacitors driven by a simple V/2 scheme, let each write flip up to 1% of half-selected cells, and have a write-then-scrub engine sweep the touched lines with a strong code before errors accumulate.
why: Facts 2 and 7: drops selectors and multi-level V/3 drivers (simpler periphery), enabling 16 decks of transistor-free cells at an effective ~0.25F2 per bit.

title: Setun balanced-ternary charge in 3D cells around the half-VDD plate
idea: Revive the Soviet Setun ternary computer: each 3D cell holds negative, zero or positive charge relative to the existing VDD/2 plate (1.58 bits/cell), read by a two-threshold sense amp; the narrowed margin causes ~1% level confusions, absorbed by a ternary BCH code over GF(3).
why: Density: +58% bits per tier without extra layers or taller capacitors; ~45% net after code overhead.

title: Two-out-of-five constant-weight codes enable reference-free ranked sensing
idea: Revive the IBM 650 / Bell relay 2-out-of-5 code: each group of n cells is written as a constant-weight word and sensed by picking the k strongest cells with a winner-take-all comparator instead of a fixed reference, so tier-to-tier Vt shifts and common leakage cancel. Residual ~1% rank flips are fixed by an outer code.
why: Facts 2 and 3: no dummy/reference bitlines and ~4x longer retention because drift becomes common-mode; tolerates poorly matched 3D tiers.

title: Delta-modulation encoding for AI tensors in error-prone 3D strings
idea: Revive Bell Labs' 1946 delta modulation: store KV-cache and activation sequences as 1-bit delta streams along the token axis across vertical tiers, so each cell's bit is worth one small step and a 1% cell BER adds only ~1% amplitude noise; the controller integrates on read.
why: Facts 1 and 5: lets marginal ~2 fF cells hold AI working sets; ~3x denser cells outweigh the ~1.5-2x bit overhead of delta coding for correlated tensors.

title: Gaines stochastic bitstreams multiplied by ANDing vertical tier strings
idea: Revive Gaines' 1960s stochastic computing: weights and activations are stored as random bitstreams laid along vertical strings, so multiplying two values is a single AND of two strings sensed together in the array, and a 1% cell BER shifts a value by only ~1%.
why: Fact 5: avoids moving operands off-die for low-precision ops (>=5x less data-movement energy) on cheap, error-prone tiers.

title: Holographic Hadamard spreading of words across 64 tiers
idea: Revive holographic memory's trick of spreading each bit over the whole hologram: apply a Walsh-Hadamard transform across 64 tiers before writing, so 1% scattered cell errors, or one whole failed tier, become sparse errors recovered by sparse-error (compressed-sensing) decoding after the inverse transform.
why: Facts 2 and 9: tolerates tier-correlated failures and row-hammer flips without per-tier spares, letting marginal tiers ship.

title: Audio-RAM revival: stack fab fallout dies onto ECC base die
idea: Revive 1980s 'ARAM' (partly failing DRAM sold for answering machines) and Sinclair's half-good chips: buy wafer-sort fallout and retired dies whose cells fail at up to 1%, hybrid-bond them onto a logic base die with strong LDPC and remap tables, and sell the stacks as CXL capacity.
why: Scarce supply: raises usable DRAM bits ~5-10% with zero new fab capital; base-die correction hides the 1% BER from hosts.

title: Williams-tube margin raster: scrub weak charges, stretch refresh 16x
idea: Williams tubes kept their spots alive by continuous raster regeneration; revive it as a base-die scrub engine that sweeps 3D tiers with a three-level sense (strong-1, weak-1, 0), rewrites only weak cells, and lets the refresh interval stretch until ~1% of cells have leaked, which the code then corrects.
why: Fact 3: refresh energy and bandwidth loss fall ~10x (64 ms toward ~1 s) by tolerating the leakage tail instead of designing for it.

title: Complementary twin cells on adjacent tiers cancel stack variation
idea: Revive IBM's balanced-capacitor read-only store and early twin-cell DRAM: store each bit as opposite charges in vertically adjacent tiers on the same pillar and sense differentially, so tier-correlated etch and doping variation cancels and a ~1% single-ended raw BER becomes ~1e-6 at the pair.
why: Facts 1 and 2: Cs can drop ~2x and tiers can thin, since differential sensing doubles signal; relaxes the 3D capacitor requirement.

title: Saturn-V voting plus Whirlwind marginal checking per tier band
idea: Revive Whirlwind's marginal checking (stressing voltages to expose weak parts) and the Saturn V LVDC's triple voting: at boot and periodically the controller lowers array voltage per tier band to measure margin, then runs strong tiers raw at up to 1% cell BER under the normal code and weak top/bottom tiers in 3-way voted mode.
why: Fact 2: no tier is discarded, so a 128-tier stack with uneven etch still yields; density loss <10% versus scrapping wafers.

title: Seven-track tape parity rebuilt as a physical 3D product code
idea: Revive 1950s tape drives' lateral-plus-longitudinal parity: one parity tier per 16 tiers plus parity pillars per row put every bit in row, column and tier codewords, decoded iteratively to correct 1% scattered cell errors along all three axes.
why: Facts 2 and 9: corrects at 1% raw BER with ~15-20% overhead while localizing wordline shorts and row-hammer bursts.

title: Weimer's 1962 TFT reborn: panel-fab memory on Gen-8 glass
idea: Revive RCA's thin-film transistor for memory: build 4-tier oxide-TFT DRAM-like arrays on Gen-8.5 glass in idle LCD and plasma panel fabs at ~1 um features, accept 1% defective cells across huge panels with block codes, and sell them as cheap capacity modules.
why: Capital intensity and U.S./allied manufacturability: panel fabs cost ~100x less per m2 than DRAM wafers; at 4 tiers cost could approach ~$10/GB with no EUV or quartz crucibles.

title: Toshiba chain FeRAM stood vertically as 3D ferroelectric strings
idea: Revive Toshiba's 1997 chain FeRAM, where each cell's transistor shunts its own ferroelectric capacitor in a series chain: build it as a vertical string of 32 shunted capacitors per pillar, 3D-NAND style, and accept ~1% read-disturb flips in neighbours that a per-string code corrects on write-back.
why: Facts 2 and 4: a 3D ferroelectric cell with one channel hole per 32 bits; error tolerance lets mismatched shunt devices and thin HZO work.

title: Optane's abandoned threshold-switch stack reused for capacitor crosspoint DRAM
idea: Revive the shelved 3D XPoint selector process: pair an Ovonic threshold switch with a tiny MIM capacitor (1S1C) in stacked crosspoint decks so the selector replaces the access transistor; OTS threshold scatter and leakage cause ~1% cell errors that tile-level codes correct.
why: Facts 1, 2 and 4: stackable charge cells with no transistors, built on existing deck-process know-how; 4 decks give ~4x bits per mask set.

title: Bucket-brigade analog strings storing multilevel weights in tiers
idea: Revive the 1969 Philips bucket-brigade delay line from echo pedals: vertical strings of discrete capacitor-plus-transistor stages pass analog charge packets holding 4-bit levels, read by a string-foot ADC, with ~1% level errors from charge loss tolerated by inference weights.
why: Density: 4 bits per stage on cheap tiers for AI weights and activations, ~3-4x bits per area versus binary DRAM.

title: Apollo restart protection: recompute tensors instead of storing them perfectly
idea: Revive the Apollo guidance computer's restart groups, which recovered from faults by re-running from checkpoints: data in 1%-BER 3D memory carry a light detection code, and on a detected-uncorrectable error the runtime recomputes that tensor tile from its producer kernel instead of relying on heavy ECC.
why: Cuts code overhead to ~3% and admits marginal cells; recompute is cheap for activations and KV pages, raising usable capacity.

title: ZettaCore redox-molecule capacitors multiply charge per 3D node
idea: Revive ZettaCore's abandoned porphyrin memory: graft a monolayer of redox molecules onto each 3D cell's storage electrode so charge is held at discrete oxidation potentials (~10x areal charge versus a dielectric at the same voltage, multi-bit), accepting ~1% molecular-variation errors.
why: Fact 1: lifts the capacitor charge wall without AR 115 or k 70; short capacitors make 3D tiers practical.

title: Catt-spiral wafer-scale stacks bonded without known-good-die sorting
idea: Revive Trilogy/Anamartic wafer-scale integration and Ivor Catt's self-configuring spiral: wafer-to-wafer bond 8 whole DRAM wafers; at power-up tiles self-test and chain into a spiral that bypasses dead tiles, while live tiles tolerate up to 1% failing cells through local codes.
why: Facts 4 and 6: no dicing, known-good-die test or per-die TSV assembly; W2W stacking cost per bit drops ~20-30% and compound stack-yield loss disappears.

title: Drum read-retry lets tiny capacitors run at 1% sense errors
idea: Revive the drum and disk habit of re-reading on the next revolution: shrink Cs to ~2 fF so ~1% of reads are noise-limited errors, and on ECC failure re-sense the restored row with a longer bitline development time.
why: Fact 1: capacitor AR falls from ~70:1 toward ~30:1 with ~2.5x less charge; rare retries cost <2% bandwidth.

title: SAGE-style federal anchor order for error-tolerant U.S. memory stacks
idea: SAGE's huge core-memory order drove core prices down ~100x and built U.S. core factories; revive it as a multiyear federal purchase commitment for 'grade-T' 3D memory specified at up to 1% raw cell BER with on-stack correction, made in U.S. mature-node fabs.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: guaranteed volume justifies cheaper tolerant fabs without EUV, raising domestic share from ~1-2%.

title: Anodic alumina pores self-assemble litho-free 3D cell arrays
idea: Revive the 1950s Keller anodic aluminum oxide pore process used in electrolytic capacitors: anodize thick aluminum into self-ordered ~25-40 nm pitch vertical pores that template capacitor and channel pillars without lithography, accepting ~1% irregular or merged pores as failed cells.
why: Fact 4: removes EUV/immersion litho layers from the cell array, cutting capital per bit with abundant aluminum.
